plan.contextChunk: This figure is a single labeled diagram of a simple pendulum hanging from a beige horizontal bar. A dashed vertical drops from the attachment point to mark the equilibrium direction, and a solid line making an angle labeled theta with it runs down and to the right; the string is labeled L and a small gray sphere at its lower end is labeled m. A dashed arc labeled s connects the equilibrium line to the bob. A dark blue arrow along the string points from the bob back toward the pivot, labeled F_T. Three red arrows leave the bob: one straight down labeled w = mg, one continuing along the string away from the pivot labeled -mg cos theta with theta marked between it and the weight arrow, and one tangent to the arc pointing back toward equilibrium labeled -mg sin theta. Axes at the upper right define +y along the string toward the pivot and +x tangent to the arc away from equilibrium. The arrow arrangement resolves the weight into components along and across the string. The diagram identifies the tangential component as the restoring force behind the oscillation.

interactionPlan.concept: A pendulum's weight resolves into a component along the string (balanced by tension) and a tangential component −mg sin θ that always points back toward equilibrium, acting as the restoring force that drives oscillation.
elements: Beige horizontal ceiling bar across the top of the figure
Pivot point where the string attaches to the ceiling
Dashed vertical line from pivot downward marking the equilibrium direction
Solid string line from pivot to bob, labeled L
Angle arc and label θ between the dashed vertical and the string, near the pivot
Gray shaded sphere (bob) at the end of the string, labeled m
Dashed arc from the bottom of the equilibrium line to the bob, labeled s (arc length displacement)
Dark blue arrow along the string from the bob toward the pivot, labeled F_T (tension)
Red arrow straight down from the bob, labeled w = mg
Red arrow from bob along the string direction away from the pivot, labeled −mg cos θ
Red arrow from bob tangent to the arc, pointing back toward equilibrium, labeled −mg sin θ
Small angle arc labeled θ between the weight arrow and the −mg cos θ arrow
Local axis pair at upper right: +y arrow along the string toward the pivot, +x arrow tangent to the arc away from equilibrium
Dashed construction lines (parallelogram) showing the weight decomposed into its two components
Optional overlay curve/label comparing sin θ to θ for the small-angle toggle
Legend keying blue = tension, red = gravity and its components

interactions.teaches: That as displacement grows, the tangential component −mg sin θ grows and always points back toward equilibrium, while the radial component −mg cos θ shrinks — and both vanish/maximize at predictable angles.
interactions.label: Angular displacement θ (degrees)

interactions.teaches: That the restoring force flips direction each time the bob crosses equilibrium, so the bob is always pulled back toward the center — the signature of oscillatory motion.
interactions.label: Release the pendulum

interactions.teaches: That replacing sin θ with θ (small-angle approximation) makes the restoring force linear in displacement — the condition for simple harmonic motion — and that the approximation fails visibly at large angles.
interactions.label: Restoring force model

demo_steps.title: The pendulum at rest
demo_steps.narration: At θ = 0 the bob hangs on the dashed vertical. The weight w = mg points straight down along the string and is entirely balanced by the tension F_T — there is no tangential force, so nothing accelerates the bob.

demo_steps.title: Displace the bob and split the weight
demo_steps.narration: Drag θ out to 25°. The weight now splits into −mg cos θ along the string (opposed by tension) and −mg sin θ tangent to the arc. Only the tangential piece is unbalanced, and it points back toward equilibrium along −x.

demo_steps.title: Push to a large angle
demo_steps.narration: At 60° the tangential arrow is long and the radial arrow has shrunk. Notice the restoring force grows with displacement — but not in proportion to it, because it follows sin θ, not θ.

demo_steps.title: Sign flip through equilibrium
demo_steps.narration: Release the bob and watch. Each time it crosses the dashed vertical the tangential arrow reverses direction, so the force always points back toward the center — this is what sustains the oscillation.

demo_steps.title: The small-angle approximation
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the compare view. Below about 15° the −mg θ arrow overlaps the −mg sin θ arrow almost exactly: the restoring force is proportional to displacement, so the pendulum is a simple harmonic oscillator with period T = 2π√(L/g).

demo_steps.title: Where the approximation breaks
demo_steps.narration: Push θ back out to 50° with both models drawn. The two arrows now visibly disagree — the true restoring force is weaker than the linear estimate, the motion is no longer simple harmonic, and the period lengthens.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Tension cancels only the radial part of gravity; the leftover tangential part, −mg sin θ, always points back toward the hanging position — and when θ is small enough that sin θ ≈ θ, that restoring force becomes proportional to displacement, which is exactly the definition of simple harmonic motion.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Portrait-oriented SVG diagram. A beige horizontal band spans the top as the ceiling. From a pivot near the top-center, a black dashed vertical line drops to mark equilibrium, and a solid black line runs down-and-right to the bob, labeled L near its midpoint. A small arc with label θ sits between the dashed vertical and the string at the pivot. The bob is a small radially-shaded gray sphere labeled m to its right. A black dashed arc labeled s sweeps from the foot of the dashed vertical to the bob. A dark navy-blue arrow runs from the bob back up along the string, labeled F_T. Three red/crimson arrows emanate from the bob: straight down labeled w = mg; along the string extended away from the pivot labeled −mg cos θ; and tangent to the arc pointing back toward equilibrium (down-and-left) labeled −mg sin θ. A small arc labeled θ sits between the vertical weight arrow and the −mg cos θ arrow. Upper right shows a thin black axis pair: +y arrow parallel to the string pointing toward the pivot, +x arrow perpendicular to it pointing away from equilibrium. Arrow lengths must scale live with θ: the tangential arrow ∝ sin θ, the radial arrow ∝ cos θ, weight arrow constant. In the compare mode draw the small-angle arrow in a lighter orange overlaid on the exact crimson arrow with a bracket showing the discrepancy, plus a small readout of sin θ vs θ in radians. Negative θ mirrors the whole construction to the left of the dashed vertical. Color key: navy = tension, crimson = gravity and components, orange = linear approximation, gray/black = geometry.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for angle theta: the learner drags the bob along the arc, the displacement s and the -mg sin theta and -mg cos theta components update in length and direction, making clear that the tangential component is the restoring force toward equilibrium.
- Animation for pendulum motion: the learner starts the swing, the bob oscillates while the velocity and restoring-force arrows change sign through equilibrium, making clear how the force continually points back toward the center of the motion.
- Toggle between exact and small-angle views: the learner switches from -mg sin theta to the small-angle form proportional to theta, the tangential-force label and approximation range update, making clear when the pendulum behaves like simple harmonic motion.

authoredContext:
A simple pendulum is defined to have a point mass, also known as the pendulum bob, which is suspended from a string of length L with negligible mass (the figure). Here, the only forces acting on the bob are the force of gravity (i.e., the weight of the bob) and tension from the string. The mass of the string is assumed to be negligible as compared to the mass of the bob.

A simple pendulum has a small-diameter bob and a string that has a very small mass but is strong enough not to stretch appreciably. The linear displacement from equilibrium is s, the length of the arc. Also shown are the forces on the bob, which result in a net force of −mgsinθ toward the equilibrium position—that is, a restoring force.

In the figure, a horizontal bar is shown. A string of length L extends from the bar at an angle theta counterclockwise from the vertical. The vertical direction is indicated by a dashed line extending down from where the string is attached to the bar. A circular bob of mass m is attached to the lower end of the string. The arc from the mass to the vertical is indicated by another dashed line and is a length s. A red arrow showing the time T of the oscillation of the mob is shown along the string line toward the bar. A coordinate system is shown near the bob with the positive y direction aligned with the string and pointing toward the pivot point and the positive x direction pointing tangent to the arc and away from the equilibrium position. An blue arrow from the bob toward the pivot, along the string, is labeled F sub T. A red arrow from the bob pointing down is labeled w = m g. A red arrow pointing tangent to the arc and toward equilibrium, in the minus x direction, is labeled minus m g sine theta. A red arrow at an angle theta counterclockwise from w is labeled minus m g cosine theta.

Consider the torque on the pendulum. The force providing the restoring torque is the component of the weight of the pendulum bob that acts along the arc length. The torque is the length of the string L times the component of the net force that is perpendicular to the radius of the arc. The minus sign indicates the torque acts in the opposite direction of the angular displacement:

discrepancies: Generated figure adds an in-canvas legend (bottom-left) and a white readout box (θ, sin θ, |F|) that do not exist in the source, plus faint gray dashed parallelogram construction lines from the component tips to the weight tip — extra chrome that changes the overall composition versus the clean source diagram.

The 'F_T' label is set as a full-size 'F' with a separate small 'T' offset to the lower-right, reading slightly awkwardly compared to the source's clean italic subscript, and it sits above-right of the arrow rather than beside its midpoint.

The '−mg sin θ' label uses a light dashed leader line back to the arrow tip; in the source the label sits directly under the arrow without a leader, so the figure reads as slightly busier around the arc/'s' region.

The +x/+y local axis cross rotates with θ in the generated version, whereas in the source it is drawn in a fixed tilted orientation next to the bob; at large θ this can make the axes disagree visually with the reader's expectation of the static source inset.
Bob radius and arrow lengths are somewhat smaller relative to string length L than in the source, so the force triangle at the bob is more compressed.
evaluation.notes: Structurally an excellent reproduction of the free-body pendulum figure (dashed vertical, θ arcs, L, arc s, navy F_T, three crimson weight vectors, m, local axes) with genuinely deep interactions (θ slider, exact/small-angle/compare model toggle, physical swing animation, 6-step narrated demo, per-arrow popups); the main weaknesses are added in-canvas clutter (legend, readout box, construction dashes) not present in the source, small legend/readout type, and a tooltip claiming F_T = mg cos θ which is only true statically, not during the animated swing.
action_items: Move the legend and numeric readout box out of the drawing area (into the side UI panel, which already shows the same numbers) so the default step-0 view is a drop-in replacement for the static source image.

Render 'F_T' as a single text node with a proper <tspan> subscript (or baseline-shifted glyph) positioned beside the arrow midpoint as in the source, and increase legend/readout font size to ≥12px if kept on canvas.

Drop or heavily de-emphasise the gray dashed parallelogram construction lines and the leader line on the '−mg sin θ' label at the default 25° state; reveal them only when the user explicitly requests the decomposition step.
Fix the tension tooltip text to state F_T = mg cos θ + mv²/L (reducing to mg cos θ only at the turning points / at rest), so the animation does not contradict the popup.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interaction structure are right; remaining issues are implementation-level (in-canvas clutter, subscript rendering, leader/construction lines, tooltip text) fixable in generation.

discrepancies: The "−mg sin θ" label sits directly on top of the dashed vertical/pivot line in the generated figure (it reads as "−mg | sin θ"), whereas in the source it is clearly clear of the vertical line below the dashed arc.

The dashed arc s and its 's' label are drawn tight against the string/bob; in the source the arc is a longer, more pronounced dashed sweep from the vertical down to the bob with 's' set above it with more clearance.

The local +x/+y axis cross is smaller and rotates with θ; in the source it is a fixed, slightly larger annotation to the upper right with longer stems, so the generated version reads as a minor decorative mark rather than the labelled frame in the original.

evaluation.notes: A near drop-in replacement for the source figure with correct vector decomposition, colors, and labels, backed by a rich and genuinely pedagogical set of controls (θ slider, force-model selector, construction toggle, live swing, 6 demo steps); the only real weaknesses are a label/dashed-line collision on −mg sin θ, a cramped arc-s annotation, and a stray garbled character in one popup.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interaction structure are correct; remaining issues are concrete rendering defects (label/line collision, cramped arc annotation, stray garbled character) that belong to the generator.

demo_steps.narration: Push θ back out to 50° with both models drawn. The two arrows now visibly disagree — the true restoring force is weaker than the linear estimate, the motion is no longer simple harmonic, and the period lengthens.

plan.keyInsight: Tension cancels only the radial part of gravity; the leftover tangential part, −mg sin θ, always points back toward the hanging position — and when θ is small enough that sin θ ≈ θ, that restoring force becomes proportional to displacement, which is exactly the definition of simple harmonic motion.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Portrait-oriented SVG diagram. A beige horizontal band spans the top as the ceiling. From a pivot near the top-center, a black dashed vertical line drops to mark equilibrium, and a solid black line runs down-and-right to the bob, labeled L near its midpoint. A small arc with label θ sits between the dashed vertical and the string at the pivot. The bob is a small radially-shaded gray sphere labeled m to its right. A black dashed arc labeled s sweeps from the foot of the dashed vertical to the bob. A dark navy-blue arrow runs from the bob back up along the string, labeled F_T. Three red/crimson arrows emanate from the bob: straight down labeled w = mg; along the string extended away from the pivot labeled −mg cos θ; and tangent to the arc pointing back toward equilibrium (down-and-left) labeled −mg sin θ. A small arc labeled θ sits between the vertical weight arrow and the −mg cos θ arrow. Upper right shows a thin black axis pair: +y arrow parallel to the string pointing toward the pivot, +x arrow perpendicular to it pointing away from equilibrium. Arrow lengths must scale live with θ: the tangential arrow ∝ sin θ, the radial arrow ∝ cos θ, weight arrow constant. In the compare mode draw the small-angle arrow in a lighter orange overlaid on the exact crimson arrow with a bracket showing the discrepancy, plus a small readout of sin θ vs θ in radians. Negative θ mirrors the whole construction to the left of the dashed vertical. Color key: navy = tension, crimson = gravity and components, orange = linear approximation, gray/black = geometry.

discrepancies: F_T is rendered in navy in the generated figure while the source prints the label in black (only the tension arrow itself is navy); a small colour-coding deviation.

The left cluster near the bob (s, −mg sin θ, the bob-angle θ) is tighter than in the source, with the −mg sin θ text sitting almost on top of the tangential arrow shaft and its leader line, whereas the source keeps it clearly below the dashed arc.

The dashed arc marking s runs all the way to the vertical and slightly past the left of the bob region; in the source it is a shorter arc segment that terminates cleanly, so the generated version reads a little busier in that area.
The +x/+y axis pair is drawn slightly larger and closer to the figure than in the source, and rotates with θ (source shows a fixed static tilted pair) — physically defensible but a visual deviation.
evaluation.notes: An essentially drop-in replacement for the source figure — pivot, dashed vertical, angle arcs, string L, navy tension, crimson weight and its two components, bob, s arc and rotated +x/+y axes are all present with correct colours and proportions — backed by genuinely useful interactions (θ slider, exact vs small-angle toggle, decomposition construction, live swing, 6-step narrated demo); only minor label-crowding near the bob and a small F_T colour deviation hold it back.
action_items: Render the F_T label in black (as in the source) or at least match the source's typographic treatment, keeping only the arrow navy.
Increase the reserved clearance around the bob so 's', the bob-side 'θ', and '−mg sin θ' do not crowd the tangential arrow; push '−mg sin θ' further below/left along the arc as in the source.
Trim the s-arc so it stops short of the bob and the dashed vertical (as in the source) to reduce clutter, and drop the faint grey leader line when the label already sits adjacent to its arrow.
Consider keeping the +x/+y axis pair fixed in size/position (or slightly smaller and further right) so it reads as the static reference inset it is in the source.
